formulas.title: The three ratios
formulas.prompt: In a right triangle, how are sin θ, cos θ and tan θ defined?
formulas.formula:
sin θ = Opposite ÷ Hypotenuse
cos θ = Adjacent ÷ Hypotenuse
tan θ = Opposite ÷ Adjacent = sin θ ÷ cos θ

variables.meaning: the side next to θ (not the hypotenuse)
the side facing the right angle

formulas.explanation: Each ratio compares two sides as seen from the angle θ. They depend only on the angle, not on the size of the triangle.
formulas.example: Sides 3, 4, 5 with θ opposite 3: sin θ = 3/5, cos θ = 4/5, tan θ = 3/4.
formulas.commonMistake: Measuring "opposite" and "adjacent" from the wrong angle.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A ladder makes angle θ with the ground. Which ratio links its length to the height it reaches?

formulas.title: The reciprocal ratios
formulas.prompt: What are cosec θ, sec θ and cot θ?
formulas.formula:
cosec θ = 1 ÷ sin θ
sec θ = 1 ÷ cos θ
cot θ = 1 ÷ tan θ
formulas.explanation: Each is the first three ratios turned upside down.
formulas.commonMistake: Pairing sec with sin and cosec with cos: the "co" ratios pair with each other.
formulas.applicationPrompt: If cos θ = 0.8, what is sec θ?

formulas.title: Values at the standard angles
formulas.prompt: What are sin θ and cos θ at 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°?
formulas.explanation: The sines are √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2. The cosines are the same list backwards. tan θ = sin θ ÷ cos θ.
formulas.commonMistake: Swapping the sine and cosine of 30° and 60°.

formulas.title: Complementary angles
formulas.prompt: How does a ratio of (90° − θ) relate to a ratio of θ?
formulas.formula:
sin(90° − θ) = cos θ   cos(90° − θ) = sin θ
tan(90° − θ) = cot θ   sec(90° − θ) = cosec θ
formulas.explanation: The two acute angles of a right triangle add to 90°, and the side opposite one is adjacent to the other.
formulas.commonMistake: Using it when the angles add to 180°, not 90°.

formulas.title: The Pythagorean identities
formulas.prompt: Which identities hold for every angle θ?
formulas.formula:
sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
1 + tan²θ = sec²θ
1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ
formulas.explanation: The first is Pythagoras in a triangle with hypotenuse 1; divide it by cos²θ or sin²θ to get the other two.
formulas.example: sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 for every θ, so 7(sec²θ − tan²θ) = 7.
formulas.commonMistake: Writing sin θ + cos θ = 1: it is the squares that add to 1.
formulas.applicationPrompt: If sin θ = 0.6, find cos θ without knowing θ.

formulas.title: From one ratio to the rest
formulas.prompt: You are told tan θ = 3/4. How do you find sin θ and cos θ?
formulas.formula:
Draw a right triangle with those two sides,
find the third side by Pythagoras,
then read off any ratio
formulas.explanation: A ratio fixes the shape of the triangle; Pythagoras completes it.
formulas.example: tan θ = 3/4: sides 3 and 4, hypotenuse 5, so sin θ = 3/5 and cos θ = 4/5.
formulas.commonMistake: Taking the hypotenuse as one of the two given sides when the ratio is a tangent.
formulas.applicationPrompt: If sec θ = 13/12, find tan θ.

formulas.title: Largest value of a sin θ + b cos θ
formulas.prompt: What are the largest and smallest values of a sin θ + b cos θ?
formulas.explanation: a sin θ + b cos θ can be rewritten as √(a² + b²) × sin(θ + α), and a sine never goes beyond ±1.
formulas.example: 3 sin θ + 4 cos θ is at most √(9 + 16) = 5.
formulas.commonMistake: Answering a + b = 7, which the expression never reaches.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Find the maximum of 5 sin θ + 12 cos θ.

formulas.title: sec θ + tan θ given
formulas.prompt: sec θ + tan θ = k. What is sec θ − tan θ?
formulas.formula:
sec θ − tan θ = 1 ÷ k
(because sec²θ − tan²θ = 1)
formulas.explanation: Factorise sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 as (sec θ + tan θ)(sec θ − tan θ) = 1.
formulas.example: sec θ + tan θ = 2 gives sec θ − tan θ = 1/2, so sec θ = 5/4 and tan θ = 3/4.
formulas.applicationPrompt: If sec θ + tan θ = 3, find tan θ.

formulas.title: Degrees, radians and arc length
formulas.prompt: How do you turn degrees into radians and back, and how long is the arc an angle θ cuts off?
formulas.formula:
π radians = 180°
Radians = degrees × π/180
Degrees = radians × 180/π
Arc length l = rθ (θ in radians)

variables.meaning: the angle at the centre, in radians

formulas.explanation: One radian is the angle whose arc is exactly one radius long. A full turn has an arc of 2πr, so a full turn is 2π radians = 360°, and π radians = 180°. In radians the angle is simply arc ÷ radius.
formulas.example: 150° = 150 × π/180 = 5π/6 radians. An arc of radius 12 cm at 5π/6 is 12 × 5π/6 = 10π ≈ 31.4 cm.
formulas.commonMistake: Multiplying by 180/π when going from degrees to radians, or putting degrees straight into l = rθ.

formulas.title: Sum and difference of two angles
formulas.prompt: What are sin(A ± B), cos(A ± B) and tan(A ± B)?
formulas.formula:
sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B
tan(A ± B) = (tan A ± tan B) ÷ (1 ∓ tan A tan B)
With B = A: sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A, cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A
formulas.explanation: These turn an awkward angle into two standard ones: 15° = 45° − 30°, 75° = 45° + 30°. Watch the signs in the cosine: cos(A + B) has a minus, cos(A − B) a plus.
formulas.commonMistake: Splitting sin(A + B) into sin A + sin B: sin 75° is not sin 45° + sin 30°.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Find sin 75° from the standard angles.

formulas.title: Greatest and least values
formulas.prompt: Between what values do a sin θ + b cos θ, a sin²θ + b cos²θ and a² tan²θ + b² cot²θ lie?
formulas.formula:
a sin θ + b cos θ: from −√(a² + b²) to √(a² + b²)
a sin²θ + b cos²θ: between a and b
a² tan²θ + b² cot²θ ≥ 2ab
sin²θ + cosec²θ ≥ 2
formulas.explanation: a sin θ + b cos θ = √(a² + b²) sin(θ + α), and a sine stays between −1 and 1. a sin²θ + b cos²θ = b + (a − b) sin²θ, and sin²θ runs from 0 to 1. When two positive terms have a fixed product (tan²θ × cot²θ = 1), AM ≥ GM makes their sum at least 2√(product), reached when the terms are equal.
formulas.example: 9 tan²θ + 4 cot²θ ≥ 2 × 3 × 2 = 12 (at tan²θ = 2/3); 5 sin²θ + 2 cos²θ lies from 2 to 5.
formulas.commonMistake: Answering a + b: 3 sin θ + 4 cos θ never reaches 7, and 9 tan²θ + 4 cot²θ is not least at 13.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Find the least value of 16 tan²θ + 25 cot²θ.

formulas.title: The 15° and 75° values
formulas.prompt: What are sin 15°, cos 15°, tan 15° and tan 75°?
formulas.explanation: Each comes from 45° ± 30°. A quick check: tan 15° must be less than 1, so it is 2 − √3 ≈ 0.27; and tan 15° × tan 75° = 1 because the angles are complementary.
formulas.commonMistake: Swapping 2 − √3 and 2 + √3: tan 75° is the big one, about 3.73.

formulas.title: cosec θ + cot θ given
formulas.prompt: cosec θ + cot θ = k. What is cosec θ − cot θ?
formulas.formula:
cosec θ − cot θ = 1 ÷ k
(because cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1)
Then cosec θ = (k + 1/k) ÷ 2, cot θ = (k − 1/k) ÷ 2
formulas.explanation: cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1 factorises as (cosec θ + cot θ)(cosec θ − cot θ) = 1, so the two are reciprocals. Adding and subtracting them gives cosec θ and cot θ, and from those every other ratio.
formulas.example: cosec θ + cot θ = 3: cosec θ − cot θ = 1/3, so cosec θ = 5/3, cot θ = 4/3, and cos θ = cot θ ÷ cosec θ = 4/5.
formulas.commonMistake: Mixing it up with sec θ + tan θ: here k = (hypotenuse + adjacent) ÷ opposite.
formulas.applicationPrompt: If cosec θ + cot θ = 5, find sin θ.

formulas.title: Complementary chains
formulas.prompt: What are tan 1° × tan 2° × … × tan 89° and sin²1° + sin²2° + … + sin²89°?
formulas.formula:
tan 1° × tan 2° × … × tan 89° = 1
sin²1° + sin²2° + … + sin²89° = 44½
(pair θ with 90° − θ)
formulas.explanation: tan(90° − θ) = cot θ, so each pair multiplies to 1 and tan 45° = 1 is left. sin²(90° − θ) = cos²θ, so each pair adds to 1: 44 pairs, plus sin²45° = 1/2.
formulas.example: sin²5° + sin²10° + … + sin²85°: 17 terms make 8 pairs and sin²45°, so the sum is 8½.
formulas.commonMistake: Forgetting the unpaired middle term sin²45° = 1/2, or counting it as 1.

formulas.title: Equations at standard angles
formulas.prompt: For an acute θ, how do you solve sin θ + cos θ = √2, tan θ + cot θ = 2 or a quadratic such as 2 sin²θ − 3 sin θ + 1 = 0?
formulas.formula:
sin θ + cos θ = √2 or tan θ + cot θ = 2 ⇒ θ = 45°
sin A = cos B (both acute) ⇒ A + B = 90°
Quadratic in one ratio: factorise, keep only roots the ratio can take
formulas.explanation: sin θ + cos θ = √2 sin(θ + 45°) reaches √2 only at θ = 45°; tan θ + cot θ = 2 gives (tan θ − 1)² = 0. In a quadratic, treat the ratio as x, factorise, and throw out roots the ratio cannot take for an acute angle (sin θ and cos θ lie strictly between 0 and 1, tan θ is positive).
formulas.example: 2 sin²θ − 3 sin θ + 1 = 0 ⇒ (2 sin θ − 1)(sin θ − 1) = 0 ⇒ sin θ = 1/2 or 1. sin θ = 1 means θ = 90°, not acute, so θ = 30°.
formulas.commonMistake: Keeping a root the ratio cannot take, such as sin θ = 1 (θ = 90°, not acute) or cos θ = 2.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Solve tan θ + cot θ = 2 for acute θ.

levels.title: Ratios of a Right Triangle
levels.description: Three ratios, five standard angles and one identity that holds everything together.

blocks.title: Name the sides from the angle
blocks.body: In a right triangle, pick one of the acute angles and call it θ. The side facing θ is the opposite side, the side next to θ (other than the longest) is the adjacent side, and the side facing the right angle is the hypotenuse.

blocks.title: SOH CAH TOA
blocks.body:
sin θ = Opposite ÷ Hypotenuse
cos θ = Adjacent ÷ Hypotenuse
tan θ = Opposite ÷ Adjacent
blocks.caption: The ratios depend only on the angle, not on how big the triangle is.

blocks.title: A 3-4-5 triangle
blocks.body: With θ opposite the side of 3: sin θ = 3/5, cos θ = 4/5, tan θ = 3/4.

blocks.title: The standard angles
blocks.body: For 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°, the sines are √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2 and √4/2: that is 0, 1/2, 1/√2, √3/2 and 1. The cosines are the same list read backwards, and tan θ = sin θ ÷ cos θ.
sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 for every angle: it is Pythagoras in a triangle whose hypotenuse is 1. Questions that look like hard calculations often collapse to this.

levels.title: Trigonometry Formulas
levels.description: The ratios, the standard values, complementary angles and the identities.

levels.title: Ratios and Standard Values
levels.description: Read ratios off a triangle and use the standard-angle table.

levels.title: Complementary Angles and One-Ratio Problems
levels.description: Pair angles that add to 90°, and build a triangle from a single ratio.

levels.title: Identities in Action
levels.description: sec θ + tan θ, largest values, and expressions built from one ratio.

levels.title: Mixed Trigonometry Practice
levels.description: A mix from the whole topic, including fresh generated questions.

levels.title: Advanced: Radians, Compound Angles and Greatest Values
levels.description: Radian measure and arcs, the 15° and 75° values, identity tricks, greatest and least values, and simple equations.

blocks.title: Measuring an angle by its arc
blocks.body: Turn a radius about the centre of a circle. The angle it turns can be measured in degrees, or by the arc its tip draws: one radian is the angle whose arc is exactly one radius long. A full turn draws the whole circumference, 2πr, so a full turn is 2π radians. Half a turn gives the rule everything else follows from: π radians = 180°.

blocks.title: Degrees, radians and arcs
blocks.body:
π radians = 180°
Radians = degrees × π/180
Degrees = radians × 180/π
Arc length l = rθ (θ in radians)
blocks.caption: l = rθ needs θ in radians. With degrees, use l = (θ/360) × 2πr instead.

blocks.title: Clocks and polygons in radians
blocks.body: A minute hand turns 6° a minute, so in 20 minutes it turns 120° = 2π/3 radians; a 21 cm hand sweeps an arc of 21 × 2π/3 = 14π = 44 cm (π = 22/7). Each exterior angle of a regular hexagon is 360° ÷ 6 = 60° = π/3, so each interior angle is π − π/3 = 2π/3.

blocks.title: New angles from standard ones
blocks.body: 15° and 75° are not in the table, but 15° = 45° − 30° and 75° = 45° + 30°. The sum and difference formulas build their values from the table. Putting B = A gives the double-angle forms, which turn sin 15° cos 15° into ½ sin 30°.

blocks.title: Sum and difference formulas
blocks.body:
sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B
tan(A ± B) = (tan A ± tan B) ÷ (1 ∓ tan A tan B)
tan 15° = 2 − √3, tan 75° = 2 + √3
blocks.caption: sin 15° = cos 75° = (√3 − 1)/(2√2) and cos 15° = sin 75° = (√3 + 1)/(2√2).

blocks.body: To tell 2 − √3 from 2 + √3, remember tan 15° is less than tan 45° = 1, so it is the small one, about 0.27. And tan 15° × tan 75° = 1, because 15° + 75° = 90°.

blocks.title: Identity tricks the SSC way
blocks.body: Each Pythagorean identity factorises: sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 means sec θ − tan θ = 1/(sec θ + tan θ), and cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1 means cosec θ − cot θ = 1/(cosec θ + cot θ). Given one of the pair, you get the other at once; adding and subtracting then gives each ratio. Long chains of angles collapse when you pair θ with 90° − θ.

blocks.title: Two chains and a pair
blocks.body: tan 1° × tan 2° × … × tan 89° = 1: each tan θ meets tan(90° − θ) = cot θ, and tan 45° = 1 is left over. sin²1° + sin²2° + … + sin²89° = 44½: 44 pairs that each add to 1, plus sin²45° = 1/2. If cosec θ + cot θ = 3, then cosec θ − cot θ = 1/3, so cosec θ = 5/3, cot θ = 4/3 and cos θ = 4/5.

blocks.title: Greatest and least values
blocks.body: The simulation shows a sin θ + b cos θ as two arrows at right angles, a and b, which add to one arrow of length √(a² + b²). As θ turns, the height of its tip is the value, so the value runs from −√(a² + b²) to √(a² + b²) and never reaches a + b. With squares the rule changes: sin²θ and cos²θ share a total of 1, so a sin²θ + b cos²θ always lies between a and b. And when two terms multiply to a constant, such as a² tan²θ and b² cot²θ, AM ≥ GM makes their sum at least 2ab.

blocks.title: The ranges to know
blocks.body:
a sin θ + b cos θ: from −√(a² + b²) to √(a² + b²)
a sin²θ + b cos²θ: between a and b
a² tan²θ + b² cot²θ ≥ 2ab
sin²θ + cosec²θ ≥ 2
blocks.caption: 3 sin θ + 4 cos θ peaks at 5; 5 sin²θ + 2 cos²θ lies from 2 to 5; 9 tan²θ + 4 cot²θ is least at 12.

blocks.title: Simple equations at standard angles
blocks.body: Exam equations are built so that θ is a standard angle. sin θ + cos θ = √2 and tan θ + cot θ = 2 both force θ = 45°. sin A = cos B with both angles acute means A + B = 90°. An equation with squares is a quadratic in one ratio: call the ratio x, factorise, and keep only the root the ratio can take.

blocks.title: A quadratic in sin θ
blocks.body: 2 sin²θ − 3 sin θ + 1 = 0 factorises as (2 sin θ − 1)(sin θ − 1) = 0, so sin θ = 1/2 or sin θ = 1. sin θ = 1 means θ = 90°, which is not acute, so θ = 30°.

For an acute θ, sin θ and cos θ lie strictly between 0 and 1 and tan θ is positive. Throw out any root outside that range before you read the angle off the table, and check you are reading the right ratio: sin θ = 1/2 is 30°, but cos θ = 1/2 is 60°.

levels.title: Practice: Radians, Identities and Equations
levels.description: Arcs and angles in radians, the 15° values, complementary chains, least values and a quadratic in cos θ.

levels.title: Challenge: Trigonometry Extension
levels.description: cosec θ + cot θ, ranges, sin 3θ = cos(θ − 6°), tan θ + cot θ = 2, and a train turning on a curve.

questions.question: In a right triangle, the side opposite θ is 5 and the hypotenuse is 13. What is sin θ?

figure.caption: A right triangle: opposite θ is 5, the hypotenuse 13
figure.ariaSummary: A right triangle with the right angle marked and the angle θ marked. The side opposite θ is 5 and the hypotenuse is 13.

questions.explanation: sin θ = Opposite ÷ Hypotenuse = 5/13.
questions.method: sin θ = Opposite ÷ Hypotenuse.

hints.text: Which two sides does the sine compare?

commonMistakes: Using the adjacent side (12) instead of the opposite one.

questions.question: What is sin 30° + cos 60°?
questions.explanation: sin 30° = 1/2 and cos 60° = 1/2, so the sum is 1.
questions.method: Use the standard-angle values.

hints.text: Both terms are equal to the same simple fraction.

commonMistakes: Taking cos 60° as √3/2.

questions.question: Which of these is equal to cos 60°?
questions.method: Complementary angles: cos θ = sin(90° − θ).

hints.text: 60° and which angle add up to 90°?

commonMistakes: Choosing sin 60°, which is √3/2.

questions.question: Which statement is true for every angle θ?
questions.explanation: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 is Pythagoras in a triangle with hypotenuse 1. The others fail: at θ = 30°, sin θ + cos θ ≈ 1.37, and tan²θ − sec²θ is always −1.
questions.method: Test a standard angle in each option.

hints.text: Try θ = 30° in each statement.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the squares: sin θ + cos θ is not 1.

questions.question: A right triangle has legs 6 and 8. θ is the angle opposite the leg of 6. What is tan θ?

figure.caption: A right triangle with legs 6 and 8
figure.ariaSummary: A right triangle with legs 6 and 8, the right angle between them marked, and the angle θ marked opposite the leg of 6.

questions.explanation: tan θ = Opposite ÷ Adjacent = 6 ÷ 8 = 0.75.
questions.method: tan θ = Opposite ÷ Adjacent.

hints.text: The tangent does not use the hypotenuse.

commonMistakes: Dividing by the hypotenuse (10).

questions.question: If sin θ = 3/5 and θ is acute, what is tan θ?

figure.caption: The right triangle sin θ = 3/5 describes
figure.ariaSummary: A right triangle with the right angle marked and the acute angle θ marked. The side opposite θ is 3 and the hypotenuse is 5.

questions.explanation: Opposite 3, hypotenuse 5, so the adjacent side is 4 (a 3-4-5 triangle). tan θ = 3/4 = 0.75.
questions.method: Draw the triangle the ratio describes and complete it with Pythagoras.

hints.text: Draw a right triangle with opposite 3 and hypotenuse 5.
The missing side is 4.

commonMistakes: Answering 3/5 again, or 4/3 (the cotangent).

questions.question: What is sin² 35° + sin² 55°?
questions.explanation: sin 55° = cos 35°, so the sum is sin² 35° + cos² 35° = 1.
questions.method: Turn one term into the complementary ratio, then use sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.

hints.text: Write sin 55° as a cosine.

commonMistakes: Trying to work out sin 35° and sin 55° on their own.

questions.question: What is 2 sin 30° × cos 30° × tan 60°?
questions.method: Substitute the standard values and multiply; the roots cancel.
commonMistakes: Taking tan 60° as 1/√3.

questions.question: If tan θ = 1/√3 and θ is acute, what is θ?
questions.method: Match the value against the standard-angle table.

hints.text: tan 60° = √3; this value is its reciprocal.

commonMistakes: Choosing 60°, whose tangent is √3.

questions.question: What is tan 10° × tan 20° × tan 70° × tan 80°?
questions.explanation: tan 80° = cot 10° and tan 70° = cot 20°. Each tangent times its cotangent is 1, so the product is 1.
questions.method: Pair angles that add to 90°.

hints.text: Which pairs of these angles add up to 90°?

commonMistakes: Adding the angles inside the tangent.

questions.question: If sec θ + tan θ = 3, what is tan θ? (to 2 decimal places)
questions.explanation: sec²θ − tan²θ = 1, so sec θ − tan θ = 1/3. Subtracting from sec θ + tan θ = 3 gives 2 tan θ = 8/3, so tan θ = 4/3 ≈ 1.33.
solutionSteps: (sec θ + tan θ)(sec θ − tan θ) = 1, so sec θ − tan θ = 1/3.
questions.method: Use sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 to get sec θ − tan θ, then subtract.

hints.text: sec²θ − tan²θ factorises.
sec θ − tan θ = 1/3.

commonMistakes: Adding the two equations instead of subtracting, which gives sec θ.

questions.question: What is the largest value 5 sin θ + 12 cos θ can take?
questions.explanation: a sin θ + b cos θ is at most √(a² + b²) = √(25 + 144) = 13.
questions.method: Largest value of a sin θ + b cos θ = √(a² + b²).

hints.text: It is not 5 + 12: the sine and cosine cannot both be 1 at once.

commonMistakes: Answering 17 = 5 + 12.

questions.question: If 5 cos θ = 4 and θ is acute, what is (sin θ + cos θ) ÷ (cos θ − sin θ)?

figure.caption: The right triangle cos θ = 4/5 describes
figure.ariaSummary: A right triangle with the right angle marked and the acute angle θ marked. The side next to θ is 4 and the hypotenuse is 5.

questions.method: Find both ratios from the 3-4-5 triangle, then substitute.

hints.text: cos θ = 4/5 describes a 3-4-5 triangle.
The fifths cancel.

commonMistakes: Computing (cos θ − sin θ) as 3/5 − 4/5.

questions.question: What is 210° in radians?
questions.explanation: π radians = 180°, so multiply by π/180: 210 × π/180 = (210/180)π = 7π/6. Check: 210° is a little more than 180°, and 7π/6 is a little more than π.
questions.method: Multiply the degrees by π/180 and simplify.

hints.text: How many degrees make π radians?
π radians = 180°, so 210° is 210/180 of π.
Simplify 210/180.

commonMistakes: Multiplying by 180/π instead of π/180, which gives 37,800/π.
Taking π as 360°, which gives 7π/12; or writing the fraction upside down, 6π/7.

questions.question: What is the value of tan 75°?
questions.explanation: 75° = 45° + 30°, so tan 75° = (tan 45° + tan 30°) ÷ (1 − tan 45° tan 30°) = (1 + 1/√3) ÷ (1 − 1/√3) = (√3 + 1)/(√3 − 1). Multiplying top and bottom by √3 + 1 gives (√3 + 1)²/2 = (4 + 2√3)/2 = 2 + √3 ≈ 3.73. It must be more than tan 60° = √3 ≈ 1.73, which rules out 2 − √3.
questions.method: Write 75° as 45° + 30° and use tan(A + B).

hints.text: Write 75° as the sum of two standard angles.
tan(A + B) = (tan A + tan B) ÷ (1 − tan A tan B), with A = 45° and B = 30°.
Rationalise (√3 + 1)/(√3 − 1) by multiplying top and bottom by √3 + 1.

commonMistakes: Giving 2 − √3, which is tan 15° (less than 1).
Adding tan 45° + tan 30° = 1 + 1/√3, as if tan(A + B) were tan A + tan B; or giving (√3 + 1)/(2√2), which is sin 75°.

questions.question: The greatest value of 3 sin θ + 4 cos θ is 7.
questions.explanation: False. 3 sin θ + 4 cos θ = 5 sin(θ + α) with 5 = √(3² + 4²), so its greatest value is 5. It could be 7 only if sin θ and cos θ were both 1 at the same θ, which never happens: when sin θ = 1, θ = 90° and cos θ = 0.
solutionSteps: The greatest value of a sin θ + b cos θ is √(a² + b²).
sin θ and cos θ cannot both be 1, because sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
questions.method: Greatest value of a sin θ + b cos θ = √(a² + b²).

hints.text: Can sin θ and cos θ both equal 1 at the same θ?
In the simulation the arrows 3 and 4 are always at right angles, so they add like the legs of a right triangle.
Work out √(3² + 4²).

commonMistakes: Adding the coefficients, 3 + 4 = 7.
Forgetting that sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 stops both from being 1 together.

questions.question: The minute hand of a clock is 21 cm long. How far, in cm, does its tip travel in 20 minutes? (Use π = 22/7.)
questions.explanation: The minute hand turns 360° in 60 minutes, which is 6° a minute, so in 20 minutes it turns 120° = 120 × π/180 = 2π/3 radians. The tip travels an arc l = rθ = 21 × 2π/3 = 14π = 14 × 22/7 = 44 cm.
questions.method: Find the angle turned, convert it to radians, then l = rθ.

hints.text: How many degrees does the minute hand turn in one minute?
In 20 minutes it turns 120°; convert that to radians.

commonMistakes: Putting 120 (the degrees) into l = rθ, which gives 2,520.
Using the hour hand's speed, ½° a minute; or giving the whole circumference, 132 cm.

questions.question: Match each angle with its measure in radians.

pairs.left: Each exterior angle of a regular decagon
Each interior angle of a regular hexagon
The angle between the hands of a clock at 3:00
The angle the minute hand turns through in 25 minutes

questions.explanation: Decagon: each exterior angle is 360° ÷ 10 = 36° = π/5. Hexagon: each interior angle is 180° − 360°/6 = 120° = 2π/3. At 3:00 the hands are a quarter-turn apart: 90° = π/2. The minute hand turns 6° a minute, so 25 minutes is 150° = 5π/6.
questions.method: Find each angle in degrees, then multiply by π/180.

hints.text: Find each angle in degrees first.
Exterior angle of a regular n-gon = 360°/n and interior = 180° − exterior; the minute hand turns 6° a minute.
Then multiply each by π/180 and simplify.

commonMistakes: Using the decagon's interior angle, 144° = 4π/5, instead of the exterior angle.
Confusing the hexagon's interior angle 2π/3 (120°) with its exterior angle π/3 (60°).

questions.question: What is the value of cos 15° − sin 15°?
questions.method: Write both from 45° − 30°; the √3 terms cancel.

hints.text: Find cos 15° and sin 15° from 45° − 30°.
Both have the same denominator, 2√2.
Subtract: the √3 terms cancel and 1 − (−1) = 2 is left.

commonMistakes: Adding instead of subtracting, which gives √6/2.
Assuming cos 15° = sin 15°, which is true only at 45°; or giving sin 15° alone, (√3 − 1)/(2√2).

questions.question: What is the value of sin²5° + sin²10° + sin²15° + … + sin²85° + sin²90°?
questions.explanation: From 5° to 85° there are 17 terms. Pair 5° with 85°, 10° with 80°, …, 40° with 50°: since sin 85° = cos 5°, each pair is sin²x + cos²x = 1, giving 8. The middle term sin²45° = 1/2 has no partner, and sin²90° = 1. Total: 8 + 1/2 + 1 = 9.5.
solutionSteps: sin²45° = 1/2 and sin²90° = 1, so the total is 9.5.
questions.method: Pair angles that add to 90°; deal with 45° and 90° on their own.

hints.text: Which angles in the list add up to 90°?
sin²(90° − x) = cos²x, so each such pair adds to 1.
Count the pairs, then add sin²45° and sin²90°.

commonMistakes: Forgetting sin²45° = 1/2, which gives 9.
Leaving out sin²90° = 1, which gives 8.5; or counting 18 terms and halving to get 9.

questions.question: What is the least value of 9 tan²θ + 4 cot²θ?
questions.explanation: tan²θ × cot²θ = 1, so the two terms multiply to 9 × 4 = 36, a constant. Two positive numbers with a fixed product have their least sum when they are equal (AM ≥ GM), so the sum is at least 2√36 = 12. It is reached when 9 tan²θ = 4 cot²θ, that is tan²θ = 2/3.
solutionSteps: AM ≥ GM: the sum is at least 2√36 = 12.
Equality at tan²θ = 2/3, so the least value is 12.
questions.method: a² tan²θ + b² cot²θ ≥ 2ab.

hints.text: What is tan²θ × cot²θ?
When two positive terms have a fixed product, their sum is least when they are equal.
The least value is 2√(9 × 4).

commonMistakes: Adding the coefficients to get 13.
Forgetting the 2 in 2√(ab), which gives 6; or working out 2 × 9 × 4 = 72, forgetting that 9 and 4 are the squares of 3 and 2.

questions.question: If 2 sin²θ + 3 cos θ − 3 = 0 and θ is acute, what is θ?
questions.explanation: Write sin²θ = 1 − cos²θ: 2 − 2 cos²θ + 3 cos θ − 3 = 0, so 2 cos²θ − 3 cos θ + 1 = 0, which factorises as (2 cos θ − 1)(cos θ − 1) = 0. cos θ = 1 gives θ = 0°, which is not acute, so cos θ = 1/2 and θ = 60°.
solutionSteps: sin²θ = 1 − cos²θ turns the equation into 2 cos²θ − 3 cos θ + 1 = 0.
(2 cos θ − 1)(cos θ − 1) = 0, so cos θ = 1/2 or 1.
cos θ = 1 gives 0°, which is not acute; cos θ = 1/2 gives θ = 60°.
questions.method: Write everything in one ratio, solve the quadratic, reject the root that is not acute.

hints.text: Write the equation in terms of cos θ only.
Use sin²θ = 1 − cos²θ; you get a quadratic in cos θ.
Factorise 2 cos²θ − 3 cos θ + 1.

commonMistakes: Reading cos θ = 1/2 as 30°, which is where sin θ = 1/2.
Keeping cos θ = 1, which gives 0°, not an acute angle; or writing sin²θ as 1 + cos²θ.

questions.question: If cosec θ + cot θ = 5 and θ is acute, what is cos θ?
questions.explanation: cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1 factorises as (cosec θ + cot θ)(cosec θ − cot θ) = 1, so cosec θ − cot θ = 1/5. Adding the two: 2 cosec θ = 26/5, so cosec θ = 13/5. Subtracting: 2 cot θ = 24/5, so cot θ = 12/5. Then cos θ = cot θ ÷ cosec θ = 12/13.
questions.method: cosec θ + cot θ and cosec θ − cot θ are reciprocals.

hints.text: Which identity links cosec θ and cot θ?
cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1 factorises, so cosec θ − cot θ = 1/5.
cos θ = cot θ × sin θ = cot θ ÷ cosec θ.

commonMistakes: Giving sin θ = 5/13 instead of cos θ.
Stopping at cot θ = 12/5; or giving sec θ = 13/12, the reciprocal of the answer.

questions.question: Which of these are true? I: the greatest value of 3 sin θ + 4 cos θ is 7. II: 5 sin²θ + 2 cos²θ always lies from 2 to 5. III: the least value of sin²θ + cosec²θ is 2.
questions.explanation: I is false: the greatest value is √(9 + 16) = 5, not 3 + 4. II is true: 5 sin²θ + 2 cos²θ = 2 + 3 sin²θ, which runs from 2 (at θ = 0°) to 5 (at θ = 90°). III is true: sin²θ × cosec²θ = 1, so by AM ≥ GM the sum is at least 2, reached at θ = 90° where both are 1.
solutionSteps: I: the greatest value is √(3² + 4²) = 5, so I is false.
II: 2 + 3 sin²θ runs from 2 to 5, so II is true.
III: x + 1/x ≥ 2 with x = sin²θ, equal at sin²θ = 1, so III is true.
questions.method: Test each statement with its own rule.

hints.text: Check each statement on its own.
a sin θ + b cos θ peaks at √(a² + b²); a sin²θ + b cos²θ lies between a and b.
For III, x + 1/x ≥ 2 for every positive x.

commonMistakes: Accepting I by adding 3 + 4.
Rejecting III by expecting the least value at sin²θ = 1/2.

questions.question: If sin 3θ = cos(θ − 6°), where 3θ and θ − 6° are both acute, what is θ in degrees?
questions.explanation: sin A = cos B with both angles acute means A + B = 90°, because sin A = cos(90° − A). So 3θ + (θ − 6°) = 90°, giving 4θ = 96° and θ = 24°. Check: 3θ = 72° and θ − 6° = 18° add to 90°.
questions.method: sin A = cos B (both acute) means A + B = 90°.

hints.text: sin A = cos B: how are A and B related when both are acute?
They add up to 90°.
Solve 3θ + θ − 6 = 90.

commonMistakes: Setting 3θ = θ − 6°, as if sin and cos were the same ratio.
Dropping the 6°: 4θ = 90° gives 22.5°; or moving the 6 the wrong way: 4θ = 84° gives 21°.

questions.question: If tan θ + cot θ = 2 and θ is acute, what is tan¹⁰θ + cot¹⁰θ?
questions.explanation: tan θ + 1/tan θ = 2 gives tan²θ − 2 tan θ + 1 = 0, that is (tan θ − 1)² = 0, so tan θ = 1 (θ = 45°) and cot θ = 1. Then tan¹⁰θ + cot¹⁰θ = 1 + 1 = 2. In fact tanⁿθ + cotⁿθ = 2 for every power n.
solutionSteps: Multiply tan θ + 1/tan θ = 2 by tan θ: tan²θ − 2 tan θ + 1 = 0.
(tan θ − 1)² = 0, so tan θ = cot θ = 1.
questions.method: Find tan θ first (it is 1), then substitute.

hints.text: Write cot θ as 1/tan θ and clear the fraction.
The quadratic is a perfect square: (tan θ − 1)² = 0.
Any power of 1 is 1.

commonMistakes: Raising the sum to the power: 2¹⁰ = 1,024.
Multiplying 2 by 10 to get 20; or using tan θ × cot θ = 1 instead of adding.

questions.question: If sin θ + cos θ = √2 cos θ and θ is acute, what is cot θ?
questions.method: Collect the cos θ terms, divide to get tan θ, then take the reciprocal.

hints.text: Collect the cos θ terms on one side.
Divide both sides by cos θ to get tan θ.
Rationalise 1/(√2 − 1) by multiplying top and bottom by √2 + 1.

commonMistakes: Stopping at tan θ = √2 − 1.
Assuming θ = 45° because of the √2 (that needs sin θ + cos θ = √2); or ignoring the cos θ on the left, which gives cot θ = 1/√2.

questions.question: A train runs at 66 km/h along a circular curve of radius 1,500 m. Through what angle, in degrees, does it turn in 10 seconds? (Use π = 22/7.)
questions.explanation: 66 km/h = 66 × 5/18 = 55/3 m/s, so in 10 seconds the train covers an arc of 550/3 m. The angle in radians is l ÷ r = (550/3) ÷ 1500 = 11/90. In degrees: 11/90 × 180/π = 11/90 × 180 × 7/22 = 7°.
solutionSteps: Speed = 66 × 5/18 = 55/3 m/s; the arc in 10 s is 550/3 m.
questions.method: Arc ÷ radius gives radians; multiply by 180/π for degrees.

hints.text: Convert the speed to m/s and find the length of arc travelled.
The angle in radians is arc ÷ radius.
Multiply by 180/π = 180 × 7/22 to get degrees.

commonMistakes: Leaving the answer in radians (11/90, about 0.12).
Using 66 km/h as if it were 66 m/s; or multiplying by π/180 instead of 180/π.
